clue.text: Coarse cloth one humps around

indicators.note: around tells us the letters of the two words are spun about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A labourer lugs bolts of rough fabric about on their back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' signals the anagram; 'Coarse cloth' at the start is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Homespun is plain rough woven fabric, originally spun and woven in the home.

clue.text: Vegetation growing beneath iron ships

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
RN, the Royal Navy, stands for a country's ships

explanation.surface: Weeds sprout under the hulls of rusting iron vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is the Royal Navy, Britain's fleet, a crossword stand-in for 'ships'.
explanation.definitionFit: A fern is a leafy plant typical of woodland undergrowth, flourishing in the shade under trees.

clue.text: Palaeolithic era discovered in the nineties?

explanation.surface: An archaeologist's find of Stone Age remains in the 1990s.
explanation.walkthrough: Palaeolithic means 'of the old stone' period, so it is an old age; and a person in their nineties is in the last stage of life.
explanation.definitionFit: Palaeolithic is literally an ancient epoch, and the nineties of one's years are the elderly stage of a life.

clue.text: Two explosive devices to be dismantled before soldiers can enter?

definitions.text: to be dismantled before soldiers can enter?

parts.note: egg is old service slang for a bomb or mine
a shell is an explosive artillery projectile

explanation.surface: Sappers must defuse a pair of bombs before troops can advance.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers here are strips of toast dipped into a boiled egg, a British breakfast habit; the top of the egg must be broken open before they can go in.
explanation.definitionFit: The brittle casing of a boiled egg has to be cracked before toast fingers can be dunked into the yolk.

clue.text: Sort of tour a carol singer's made

indicators.note: to sort letters is to arrange them, so these words are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A chorister has organised a round of carol performances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' signals the anagram of TOUR A CAROL; ''s made' only links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coloratura is a soprano who specialises in elaborate ornamented runs and trills.

clue.text: Look over half-finished lavatories in pavilion

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second

parts.note: to gaze is to look steadily

indicators.note: only half of the word survives, its last two letters dropped

parts.note: bogs is British slang for lavatories

explanation.surface: Someone peers across at half-built toilets inside a sports pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: BOGS loses its second half (GS) to leave BO; 'over' places GAZE above it in the down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gazebo is a small open garden summerhouse or pavilion with a view.

clue.text: Magazine taken by two doctors — The Hobbyist?

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a doctor

indicators.note: the magazine is taken in, held between the abbreviations for the medics

parts.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
Elle is a well-known fashion magazine

explanation.surface: A periodical is read by a pair of GPs looking for a pastime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Hobbyist' looks like a magazine title; the question mark flags that it defines by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who builds scale models of trains or aircraft is a typical pastime enthusiast.

clue.text: High level of sound emitted by bat?

explanation.surface: Squeaks come from a flying bat at a deafening pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The bat looks like the flying animal with its high-pitched squeaks, but it is the strung bat used in tennis or squash.
explanation.definitionFit: A din or loud clamour is a high level of noise, and the strung frame used in tennis to hit the ball is the other sense.

clue.text: Spherical ball, thrown high, caught by girl

indicators.note: one piece is held inside the other, as a catch is held in the hands

parts.note: gal is an informal word for a girl
a lob is a ball sent high into the air

explanation.surface: A girl catches a round ball tossed up into the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'caught by' puts the high throw inside the word for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Global can mean shaped like a globe, round like a sphere.

clue.text: Senior churchman, one immersed in study

indicators.note: one letter is plunged inside the word for the room

parts.note: a den is a private study or retreat
a means one

explanation.surface: A cathedral cleric is engrossed in scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'study' looks like a verb but is the room, DEN, with A dropped inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A dean is the head of the chapter of a cathedral, a senior clergyman.

clue.text: Used witticism the wrong way, defendant accepts

indicators.note: the word for the defendant takes in the other piece

parts.note: the accused is the defendant at a trial

indicators.note: the witticism word is read backwards

parts.note: a mot (bon mot) is a witty remark

explanation.surface: A defendant admits to having made a joke that went badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the wrong way' turns the witticism to TOM; 'accepts' puts it inside the defendant. 'Used' is the definition, as in 'used to'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being used to something means being familiar with it through habit.

clue.text: Pop a question not entirely impervious to sense?

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, a run hidden inside it

explanation.surface: Proposing marriage doesn't quite get through to a dense partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through 'POP A QUEstion'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something murky is impossible to see through or understand, closed to light and to meaning.

clue.text: Enclosed square found in Exeter or Lincoln typically

definitions.text: Enclosed square found in Exeter or Lincoln typically

parts.words: Enclosed square found in Exeter or Lincoln typically
parts.note: Exeter and Lincoln are Oxford colleges, not just cities, and a college is built around a walled courtyard

explanation.walkthrough: Exeter and Lincoln are cathedral cities, but here they are Oxford colleges, each built round an enclosed courtyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A college courtyard surrounded by buildings is the classic four-sided enclosed square.

clue.text: Lift to reveal solution

indicators.note: a solution is something dissolved and remixed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Raising a cover to unveil the answer to a puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solution' looks like the answer of a puzzle but signals the anagram of TO REVEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Elevator is the American word for a lift carrying people between floors.

clue.text: Northern hillside over in outskirts of Newry? Not far off

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the outside letters of the town
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters
the hillside word is turned over, read backwards

parts.note: brae is a Scots and northern English word for a hillside

explanation.surface: A slope near the Northern Irish town of Newry is close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' gives EARB; 'in' puts it between the outside letters of Newry, a town in Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: Something close by is only a short distance away.

clue.text: Current support for footballer — he'll make a complaint

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece goes beneath the one it holds up

parts.note: a back is a defensive player in football
AC is alternating current
he, taken from the contraction for he will

explanation.surface: A footballer, propped up by the latest equipment, keeps moaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support for' puts the current beneath the footballer, a defender; the contraction gives the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint here is an ailment, and an aching back is a common one.

clue.text: Reason pupil's inserted a few words

indicators.note: the letter for the pupil is put into the reason word

parts.note: a cause is a reason
L is a learner, as on a British L-plate

explanation.surface: A student gets a few lines into an essay to justify something.
explanation.walkthrough: L, for learner (from the L-plates British learner drivers display), goes inside CAUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A clause is a short group of words containing a verb, part of a sentence.

clue.text: Retinue mostly keen to catch joke

indicators.note: the trimmed keen word catches the joke inside itself
most of the word is kept, its last letter dropped

parts.note: eager means keen
a quip is a joke

explanation.surface: A keen entourage tries to get the punchline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims keen to EAGE; 'to catch' has it take the joke inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An equipage is the carriage, horses and attendants of a grand person, a retinue.

clue.text: Landed with spots, painful, with tops coming off

indicators.note: each word loses its first letter, its top in a down answer

parts.note: a rash is an outbreak of spots
sore means painful

explanation.surface: Someone arrives covered in sore blisters which lose their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: RASH and SORE each lose their first letter, R and S, giving ASH and ORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on dry land after a voyage, as a sailor is once off the ship.

clue.text: Expresses criticism of wine containers used by pub

parts.note: a bar is a pub
racks hold bottles of wine

explanation.surface: A drinker complains about the bottle stands in the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: To barrack is British for jeering a speaker or player.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack someone is to jeer or heckle them noisily.

clue.text: Judgement on university people about to be overturned

indicators.note: the short word for about is turned upside down in this down entry

parts.note: ca (circa) means about
men means people

explanation.surface: Academic staff are about to see their verdict reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be overturned' turns circa's abbreviation to AC, placed on top of the rest in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Acumen is keen insight, the ability to make good judgements.

clue.text: Simple calculator for keeping an account in a business

indicators.note: the business abbreviation keeps the account abbreviation inside it

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper tallies a firm's ledger with a basic counting device.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts the account inside the short form of business.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a frame of sliding beads used for basic arithmetic.

clue.text: Appeal from everybody over Yorkshire Water

indicators.note: in a down answer the first word sits over the river

parts.note: all means everybody
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Every customer lodges an appeal against the regional water company.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire Water is a real utility company, but here it is a river: the Ure flows through North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is attractiveness or charm, the appeal something holds.

clue.text: Owe gainful employment to produce from Africa — sort of pheasant

indicators.note: the words are put to a new use, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A job owed to someone so they can grow farm produce in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employment' signals the anagram of OWE GAINFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: This game bird, related to pheasants, is native to Africa.

clue.text: Do office — work it offers variety

explanation.surface: Clerical tasks provide plenty of variety.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is the clerical job of keying text; the other is a kind or sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Keyboarding letters is routine clerical work, and a sort or kind of thing is a variety.

clue.text: Body of troops one league behind

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, the British reserve force
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A unit of soldiers lags a league to the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body of troops' looks like the definition, but it is TA, the Territorial Army; 'behind' at the end is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tail as a noun can mean the rear or backside of something.

clue.text: Erica's left to consume toast

indicators.note: the plant word eats the letter for left

parts.note: Erica is the botanical genus of heath plants

explanation.surface: A woman named Erica leaves to eat her toast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erica' looks like a woman's name; it is the genus of heathers, HEATH, which takes L inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a glass with the words 'your health' is a common toast.

clue.text: Pay grannies to work?

indicators.note: putting the letters to work rearranges them into a new word

explanation.surface: Should elderly women be paid for going back to their jobs?
explanation.walkthrough: 'to work' signals the anagram of GRANNIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Earnings are the money received as pay for work.
